These are design-level gaps, which means the "shared theory" premise is weaker than the counterargument concedes — the honest ceiling is correct pattern SELECTION, unevenly ENFORCED as a matter of design, not testing.

RECOMMENDED REWRITE: keep as praise, retitle to "Six correct local pattern choices — strongest in benefit-framed toggles and consequence-stating destructive copy", lead with obs 43 (monetisation-aligned) and obs 54 (verifies a previously-UNVERIFIED §8 rule), and drop "grammar"/"system"/"shared theory" language. Add obs 7, 25, 32, 45 to the counterargument alongside 26 and 31. Severity stays praise — praise is a category, not a rung on the friction ladder, and nothing here inflates to major.

confirmed.title: The product's namesake feature is unreachable by mouse: Focus mode + Pomodoro exist only behind an undocumented keypress
confirmed.evidence: obs 22, 23; design-system.md §0 (app host is focus.toggl.com, marketing name 'Toggl Focus'); company-research.md §4 (focus mode is a listed Free-tier feature on the pricing page)
confirmed.argument: Focus mode with three timer variants (count-up, count-down, Pomodoro) has zero visible entry points in the chrome — it exists only via the F key, which is itself documented only inside the ?-panel (obs 23, 22). This is the feature the product is literally named after (the host is focus.toggl.com; the job-ad name is 'Toggl Focus') and one that the pricing page advertises as a Free-tier hook for the individual-user top of the PLG funnel. For any pointer-driven user it effectively does not exist. Worse, the failure mode for the initiated is silent: pressing F with no timer running does nothing, with no feedback (obs 23) — so even a user who reads the shortcut panel can conclude the feature is broken.
confirmed.counterargument: Chrome minimalism is Toggl's stated strategy ('no bloat', twice in their positioning — company-research §3), and focus/Pomodoro modes self-select for keyboard-centric users who will find the ?-panel. One keystroke is the ideal invocation once known. The defense collapses on 'once known', though: the only path to learning F is pressing ?, another invisible keystroke, so discovery requires already being the persona the feature is hidden for.
confirmed.verifierReasoning:
THE FACTS CHECK OUT; THE FRAMING DOES NOT.

Obs 23 supports the literal claim exactly: focus mode with three timer variants (U count-up / D count-down / O Pomodoro) has no observed entry point in the chrome, and F with no timer running is a silent no-op. Obs 22 confirms F is listed in the ?-panel. company-research §4 confirms focus mode is a listed Free-tier item. So the observable defect is real. Everything that lifts it from minor to "major" is rhetoric that the reviewer's own cited sources refute.

DEFENSE 1 — the namesake argument is factually wrong, and it is wrong on the reviewer's own evidence. design-system §0 (cited by the reviewer) says: "Copy in the UI still says 'Toggl 2.0'... Marketing name 'Toggl Focus' from the job ad does not appear in the app chrome." company-research §2 goes further: the product is "Toggl 2.0 (formerly Focus, formerly Plan)" — Focus is a DEAD name in a Plan → Focus → 2.0 chain. focus.toggl.com is a legacy hostname from a renamed product, the same way a company keeps a redirect after a rebrand. The product is not named after this feature today; it was named something adjacent two names ago. Strip that away and the headline reduces to "an optional individual-productivity mode has no mouse affordance," which is a materially smaller claim. The title also overstates its own body: obs 22 shows the keypress IS documented, in the app's own shortcuts panel. "Undocumented" is not what the evidence says.

DEFENSE 2 — Pomodoro is off-strategy, not central. The category claim is "Time Intelligence for Teams That Plan Seriously" and the thesis is "time intelligence is the foundation, not a feature" (§3). The monetisation ladder is individual tracking → team visibility → money questions (§4), and Free→Starter converts on team capacity, Starter→Premium on profitability/utilization/estimate-vs-actual. Pomodoro gates no upgrade, feeds no planning surface, and produces no data the capacity or profitability layers consume. For a bootstrapped company whose scoreboard is conversion, expansion and retention (§1), spending permanent chrome on a Free-tier attention-management gadget is precisely the "bloat" they position against twice (§3). Being on the Free feature list is not the same as being a funnel hook: on a PLG pricing table, "focus mode" is a comparison-row item that keeps the Free tier from reading thin next to Clockify and Everhour (§5). It does its job on the pricing page, not in the toolbar.

DEFENSE 3 — the chrome budget is already oversubscribed, and this sweep proves it. The Timer surface currently carries suggestion cards (obs 5), a fake-meeting calendar-connect ad (obs 6), a floating onboarding checklist that already overlaps the sidebar footer at 952px (obs 12), and spotlight tooltips (obs 13). Obs 21 flags exactly this — "three stacked mechanisms on one surface." Goals is already exiled behind an unlabelled panel toggle (obs 19). A fifth persistent affordance worsens a measured, higher-frequency problem to solve a lower-frequency one. I will not overclaim here: the running-timer state (obs 11) is craft-heavy and has room for one more small control, so this defense limits the fix's cost rather than eliminating it.

DEFENSE 4 — "zero entry points anywhere" is stronger than the evidence licenses. product-map §3 lists a settings gear in the Timer toolbar that no observation in the 57 ever opens, and the sweep is web-only — the sidebar footer "Download apps" (product-map §2) went uninspected, and Pomodoro is historically a desktop-app/extension feature in Toggl's own Track lineage. Verified: no entry point in the observed web chrome. Not verified: none anywhere in the product.

WHAT SURVIVES. Two things. (a) A pointer-driven user cannot reach an advertised feature — true, and cheap to fix with one icon in the running-timer control cluster. (b) The silent no-op is a genuine defect: a shortcut the product itself documents does nothing with no feedback. But (b) is not Focus-specific — obs 27 records the same class of failure (N silently no-ops until the page has been clicked once). This is a keyboard-layer feedback pattern, and merging obs 23 + 27 into one finding about silent shortcut failures would be stronger than attaching it to Focus mode as severity ballast.

SEVERITY. "Major" requires real friction on a path users hit weekly or more. This is not friction on a path — it is a one-time discovery gate on an optional mode, and the reviewer concedes the post-discovery invocation is ideal. Affected population: pointer-driven users who specifically want Pomodoro, a minority of a minority; for everyone else the cost is zero because they never look for it. Compare what the same sweep found on paths users genuinely hit weekly: obs 15 (a micro-entry is unreachable on the grid via click, double-click and element-targeted click — and the first entry of a user's life lands under the current-time line by definition), obs 51/16 (every duration under an hour renders "0h" in KPIs and day headers — the entire first week of a new account reads as zero), obs 32 (silent draft loss on the create-task drawer), obs 10 (dead-click after popover close inside the core timer loop). Those are weekly-or-more, core-path, and data-integrity-adjacent. Ranking Pomodoro discoverability alongside them is severity inflation. The counterargument that the ?-panel is itself invisible is weaker than presented — `?` is a near-universal convention (Gmail, GitHub, Linear, Notion, Slack), and obs 24 shows this product runs a deliberate, well-built power layer (`+`/`#`/`P1`/natural-language dates, called "Excellent Track-DNA") that self-selects the same population.

Real, worth logging, worth a one-icon fix. Minor.

confirmed.title: Auto-log time inverts discoverability: a default-on behavior that manufactures logged time is disclosed only as a ⓘ in a per-task overflow menu
confirmed.evidence: obs 36, 35; company-research.md §3 ('real data' vs 'spreadsheet guesses' is the claimed differentiator; 'time intelligence is the foundation')
confirmed.argument: Every other item in this lens is a feature users can't find. Auto-log is the reverse: a feature that finds users. The ⋮ menu shows 'Auto-log time ⓘ (Global setting active)' (obs 36) — meaning planned slots silently become logged time by default, and the entire disclosure surface for this is one small ⓘ two clicks deep on an individual task. The strategic thesis is that Toggl's planning runs on real tracked data rather than guesses; a silent plan→actual conversion means the Logged/Planned/Estimate numbers a user sees (obs 35) and reports on can contain hours nobody tracked, with no visible marker distinguishing them. For the agency ICP that bills on logged time (company-research §1), the least discoverable behavior in the product is the one with billing consequences.
confirmed.counterargument: Default-on auto-logging serves the migrated Plan user base — planners who never tracked — and maximizes data completeness, which arguably serves the time-intelligence thesis rather than undermining it. The global setting presumably has a proper home in Admin settings (untouched in this sweep, per the disclosure note), and a per-task escape hatch exists. This is a real defense of the default; it is a much weaker defense of ⓘ-only disclosure for behavior that alters billable records.
confirmed.verifierReasoning:
EVIDENCE CHECK — both cited observations exist, but one of them cuts against the finding and the other is thinner than the claim built on it.

Obs 36 records a menu string: "Auto-log time ⓘ (Global setting active), per-task toggle." That is all it records. The second sentence of obs 36 — "planned slots silently become logged time; philosophically huge" — is the observer's interpretation, and the file's own header (line 4) says explicitly: "Severity and interpretation come later — this file is evidence, not analysis." The reviewer has cited the gloss as if it were the observation.

Four load-bearing premises in the criticism are unverified by the sweep:
1. "Default-on." "Global setting active" is a status readout for one trial workspace. It does not establish a product-wide default. Nobody checked.
2. "The entire disclosure surface is one small ⓘ." Line 95 of the evidence log: "Nothing in Admin settings was touched." The reviewer is grading the adequacy of a disclosure surface the sweep explicitly declined to visit, then treating its absence from the log as evidence of absence in the product.
3. "One small ⓘ explains it." The ⓘ was never opened. design-system.md §7 lists Tooltip under "Still unverified" and §8 flags tooltips as UNVERIFIED copy. The entire severity rests on the inadequacy of text nobody read. If it says "Planned time is logged automatically when the slot passes — change for all tasks in Admin settings," the finding evaporates.
4. "No visible marker distinguishing them." Not checked at the entry level; obs 17 inventories the entry row (checkbox, $, play-again, ⋮) without addressing provenance markers.

Obs 35 actively undercuts the claim it was cited to support. The reviewer says the numbers "can contain hours nobody tracked, with no visible marker distinguishing them" — but obs 35 shows the task drawer rendering Logged / Planned / Estimate as three separately labelled, separately explained values. Obs 37 shows ESTIMATE and LOGGED as distinct Tasks-list columns; obs 52 shows LOGGED TIME and ESTIMATED TIME as distinct report columns. Keeping planned and actual visibly separate is the product's structural commitment, evidenced in three places. Citing obs 35 for the opposite proposition is a misread.

STRONGEST DEFENSE OF TOGGL:

(a) The ⋮ entry is not the disclosure surface — it is the override surface, and it is well-formed. "(Global setting active)" communicates three things at once: the behavior exists, it is inherited from a workspace default, and it can be overridden here. That is the correct pattern for scoped settings, and showing inherited state on the local override is better than most products manage. The ⓘ is system-consistent, not an evasion: obs 35 uses ⓘ on Logged/Planned/Estimate, obs 52 on Estimated time. Toggl uses ⓘ wherever a value or behavior carries a definition.

(b) The strategic argument inverts. §3's comparandum for "real data" is a spreadsheet guess — a number typed from memory at month-end. An entry derived from a slot the user personally scheduled, on a specific day, against a specific task, at a specific duration, is categorically closer to real data than that. And §2/§6: the migrated Toggl Plan base "did not choose this product — they were moved into it," from a tool with no tracking. For them the alternative to auto-log is not accurate tracking; it is zero data, which renders every Premium surface (utilization, profitability, estimate-vs-actual per §4) empty. Auto-log is the on-ramp that lets "time intelligence is the foundation" survive contact with planners. The reviewer concedes this is "a real defense of the default," then declines to weigh it.

(c) The billing-consequence framing skips two defaults-off gates and a workflow. Obs 28: Billable is a ★ premium per-task field defaulting OFF. product-map §4 confirms the gating. Members table (product-map §3): Rate `None`, Cost `None` by default — obs 45 confirms the missing input for money is a member rate, not logged time. And Toggl ships Approvals (product-map §3): "review, approve, and lock time in one place." An auto-logged entry becomes an invoiced dollar only if billable was switched on, a rate was set, and a human approval step was skipped. The agency ICP that bills on logged time is precisely the account most likely to be running Approvals. "The least discoverable behavior is the one with billing consequences" is rhetorically sharp and factually three steps removed.

(d) Frequency test fails for "major." The brief requires real friction on a weekly-or-more path. ⋮ → Auto-log is a settings-override path: touched roughly once at setup, then never. The behavior may run daily; the friction described is a one-time discovery event. Compare the genuinely weekly items in the same log — obs 15 (micro-entry unreachable on the grid, hit on your first-ever entry by definition), obs 51/16 (sub-hour durations render as "0h" across Reports KPI, day headers, and totals), obs 32 (silent draft loss on click-outside during task creation), obs 10 (dead-click after popover close in rapid timer workflows). Those clear the bar. This does not.

(e) Lens fit. The reviewer's own framing — "every other item in this lens is a feature users can't find; auto-log is the reverse" — is an argument that it does not belong in a discoverability lens at all. An aggressively active default is a defaults/consent finding, not a findability one. Including it stretches the lens rather than strengthening it.

WHAT SURVIVES: a genuine, narrow note. A behavior that writes time records — rather than merely displaying them — deserves consequence copy at the point of enablement, and Toggl's own voice standard sets that bar (design-system.md §8: empty states "explain the consequence, not just the state"). That is a legitimate question worth asking. But it is a question, not a finding, because the sweep never opened Admin settings, never read the ⓘ, never observed auto-log create an entry, and never checked whether such an entry carries provenance marking.

RULING: downgraded to minor, and it should be re-scoped as an open evidence item rather than shipped as a finding — open Admin settings, read the ⓘ text, verify the default state, and check whether an auto-logged entry is marked in the Timer list. Presenting a four-inference chain as a major finding with billing implications is exactly the kind of overreach that costs a critique its credibility when the defender opens the settings page and finds a properly worded toggle.

confirmed.title: Goals is a nav-less feature: an entire goal system lives behind an unlabeled panel toggle, with mobile vocabulary leaking through
confirmed.evidence: obs 19, 20; product-map.md §2 (no Goals entry anywhere in the four nav groups) and §3 ('what the right-hand panel contains' was flagged UNVERIFIED)
confirmed.argument: Goals — with example templates and a create flow — exists exclusively behind an unlabeled icon toggle at the far top-right (obs 19). It appears in no nav group, no route, no onboarding item. The strongest evidence of its invisibility is in the evidence itself: the product-map author, systematically walking every surface for an audit, initially logged the panel's contents as UNVERIFIED — a professional inspection missed it on first pass. Goals are a habit/retention mechanic; hidden, they cannot do that job. The '— tap to use' copy (obs 20) on a desktop surface suggests the panel was ported from mobile without a desktop discoverability pass, which would explain why it never acquired a nav identity.
confirmed.counterargument: This reads like a deliberate soft launch: keeping an experimental feature out of the nav de-risks it, and a side panel makes Goals ambient alongside any view rather than a destination. If Goals is beta, low discoverability is the point. This defense is moderately strong — but it coexists awkwardly with shipping example-goal templates, which are an adoption device, inside a surface designed not to be found.
confirmed.verifierReasoning:
The core factual claim is supported and not refutable: obs 19 states Goals lives behind the right-panel toggle and "appear nowhere else in the nav," and product-map §2's table (8 items across TRACK/ANALYZE/PLAN/MANAGE) contains no Goals entry. So this is real. But it is overweighted at major on three counts.

(1) The argument's self-described strongest evidence is factually backwards. product-map §3 inventories the Timer toolbar as "...four layout icons, a settings gear, and a right-panel toggle" — the auditor found and logged the control. The UNVERIFIED line covers "what the four layout icons switch between, and what the right-hand panel contains," flagging the plainly-visible layout icons identically in the same sentence. The doc's header defines UNVERIFIED as "not confirmed by direct inspection," i.e. not yet clicked, not undiscoverable. A professional inspection did not miss Goals; it hadn't opened the drawer yet. The load-bearing rhetorical move fails.

(2) Obs 22 is uncited and cuts against the claim: the `?` shortcuts panel lists "L side panel." The panel is documented and keyboard-addressable, so "an unlabeled icon toggle" is an incomplete account of its reach. This also breaks the mobile-port causal story — a surface ported from mobile without a desktop pass does not ship with a desktop keyboard shortcut in the desktop shortcuts panel. (The word "unlabeled" is itself unverified for accessible name; design-system §7 shows aria labels on comparable icon controls including "Toggle Sidebar.")

(3) Severity fails the stated bar. Low discoverability produces no friction for users who never find it — no broken task, no rework, no data loss. It is an adoption/activation problem, not a weekly-path friction problem. Same-log neighbors that do clear the bar: obs 15 (micro-entry unreachable on the grid, the first entry every new user creates), obs 32 (silent draft loss on outside-click), obs 51/16 (sub-hour time renders as 0h). And obs 23 is the strictly worse instance of this exact species — Focus mode with Pomodoro has no visible entry point anywhere and silently no-ops on F — while Goals has a persistent toolbar control present across views (§3 Timeline toolbar also ends in "panel toggle"). Ranking Goals major while obs 23 exists is internally inconsistent.

Defense that holds: the right rail is a system convention, not an orphan — Timeline's rail carries Unplanned tasks (obs 47), the project page's rail carries the value-framed feature toggles (obs 43), and skeletons load in it (obs 56). Goals as ambient companionship to the calendar you are logging against is arguably the correct placement for a habit mechanic; a nav destination would require leaving the timer to see the goal. A 9th nav item for a personal target is the bloat Toggl explicitly positions against twice (company-research §3, §6.4), and Goals fits none of the four existing groups cleanly — evidence the IA is coherent and Goals is a cross-cutting overlay. The reviewer's rebuttal of their own counterargument also fails: an example template is the documented inline empty-state pattern (design-system §7), not an acquisition device; a bare "+ New goal" with no model of what a goal looks like would be a worse empty state. Finally, "appears in no nav group, no route" is not fully established — Admin settings → TRACKING & RATES lists "Targets" (product-map §4), an adjacent surface the audit never opened.

Scope correction: the finding should be restated as "Goals has no route or nav identity; reach depends on a toolbar icon or the L shortcut behind ?" — a real adoption-tier IA observation, minor. The "tap to use" slip (obs 20) is genuine but polish-tier alone and is one of five vocabulary drifts in this log (obs 1 Timer/Calendar/none, obs 25 P1-P3 vs High/Medium/Low, obs 40 "Inbox", obs 55 "Time log"); it belongs in one consolidated copy-consistency finding rather than as severity ballast here, and bundling it double-counts.

confirmed.title: The shortcuts panel is load-bearing documentation hidden behind the layer it documents, and its vocabulary doesn't match the visible UI
confirmed.argument: The ?-panel is the sole place where Focus mode (obs 23), the Alt+D theme override (obs 22 — no theme control was observed anywhere else in the chrome), and the P1/P2/P3 priority tokens are documented. That single surface is itself reachable only by keystroke — circular: to discover the keyboard layer you must already be a keyboard person. And the panel underdelivers even for readers: it names priorities 'P1 P2 P3' while every visible menu says High/Medium/Low/None (obs 25), so the map doesn't match the territory. The layer then fails silently in practice — N no-ops until the page has been clicked once (obs 27), Ctrl+↵ fails from the Dates field (obs 26), F no-ops without feedback (obs 23) — so users who do cross the discovery threshold get intermittent silent failure, the exact experience that teaches people shortcuts 'don't work here'.
confirmed.counterargument: ? for shortcuts is the industry convention (Gmail, Linear, GitHub), and power layers are supposed to be self-selecting; putting them in the chrome would contradict the 'no bloat' positioning. That defends the panel's location well. It does not defend the panel being the only documentation for whole features, nor the P1/High vocabulary split, nor silent no-ops — conventions cover where reference lives, not whether the layer gives feedback.
confirmed.verifierReasoning:
EVIDENCE CHECK — the facts are real, the citations are partly stretched.

Obs 22, 23, 25, 26, 27 all say what the reviewer says they say, with two exceptions worth naming:

- Obs 22 does NOT say "no theme control was observed anywhere else in the chrome." That is the reviewer's gloss on the parenthetical "(a manual theme override exists after all)." The sweep's own disclosure section says "Nothing in Admin settings was touched," no observation anywhere records opening the avatar/profile menu (product-map §2 lists it as an unopened rail icon), and design-system open item 4 states the light theme was never rendered — i.e. the theme was never toggled through any UI. So "the ?-panel is the sole documentation for Alt+D" is unverified absence from a partial sweep, not an observed fact. One of the three legs is unsupported.
- Obs 25 supports "the priority menu says High/Medium/Low/None" (one menu, obs 30). "Every visible menu" is overreach; obs 37/39 record that priority renders in list columns and board chips but not what string they use.

THE STRONGEST DEFENSE:

1. The panel's location is conceded as conventional, and that concession does more work than the reviewer allows. The "circular discovery" argument is not an additional charge — it is a restatement of the convention they already accepted. Every ?-panel in software has exactly this property. It adds no weight.

2. "Load-bearing documentation" overstates by conflating reference with discovery. Nobody discovers Gmail's `e` from the ? panel; they discover archiving from the button and later learn the key. The correct question is per-feature, not per-panel: does each feature have a discovery path appropriate to its audience? Only one of the three named features fails that test.

3. P1/P2/P3 vs High/Medium/Low is not "the map doesn't match the territory" — it is the standard split between an **input token** and a **display label**. Linear ships precisely this (type `P1`, chip reads "Urgent"); Jira ships it; P1=highest is near-universal. A typing alphabet is optimized for keystroke economy and cross-tool familiarity, not for string-matching a mouse menu. Critically, obs 24 records that the tokens "render as chips" the instant they are typed, so the mapping is taught at point of use on the first keystroke at zero cost — and obs 24 does **not** record whether that chip reads "P1" or "High." If it reads "High," the mismatch self-resolves on first use and the criticism evaporates. The reviewer treats an unverified detail as settled. (The sharper version of this finding, which they missed: there are four priority values and three tokens — no token for "None.")

4. The silent-failure leg is three unrelated defects wearing one title, which is where the severity inflation lives. Individually: obs 27 is document-focus behavior, self-healing after a single click and impossible to hit twice in a session where the user has clicked anything — cost is one keystroke, once. Obs 26 is a Radix popover swallowing Enter in one field of one modal, and design-system §Modal records that the footer primary carries a visible `↵` hint, so the mouse path is labeled. Obs 23 is a **precondition, not a failure**: Focus mode is a mode *of a running timer* (obs 23's own submenu is F → count-up / count-down / Pomodoro), so with nothing running there is no object to focus. Silence is poor feedback, but "shortcuts don't work here" is the wrong reading of it.

5. Strategy: "no bloat" is a stated Toggl value twice over (company-research §3, §6.4), and their competitive position is explicitly against Float/Runn/Productive chrome weight. Adding visible entry points for every power feature is the exact bloat they position against.

6. Frequency test, applied strictly: the weekly loop is type description → project → play → stop → read report. None of obs 22/23/25/26/27 sits in it. The ? panel is by construction an occasional surface, and the users harmed by its discoverability are the ones who never press ? — who are unharmed in daily work because they use the mouse.

WHAT SURVIVES:

One leg, and it is not the one the title names. **Focus mode having no mouse-reachable entry point (obs 23)** is a genuine defect with strategic weight the reviewer under-argued: the app is hosted at `focus.toggl.com`, Toggl's marketing name for it is "Toggl Focus," and focus mode is a **named free-tier feature on the pricing page** (company-research §4). A feature that names the product and appears on the pricing page, with zero non-keyboard entry point, is a conversion-funnel problem, not just a UX one — free-tier users are the funnel and cannot find what the tier advertises. That deserves its own finding.

RULING:

Downgraded. The evidence is accurate but the finding is mis-titled, bundled, and over-weighted. It stacks four separable issues (panel discoverability, orphaned features, vocabulary, three unrelated no-ops) under one severity, one leg is unverified absence, one leg is defensible industry practice with an unverified detail read against the product, and nothing in the bundle touches a weekly-or-more path. Harm is one-time non-discovery, not repeated friction — a discoverability defect, which under the stated bar is minor.

Recommendation to the reviewer: split it. Drop the Alt+D leg until the avatar menu and Admin settings are actually opened. Re-scope the survivor to "Focus mode — a pricing-page free-tier feature that names the product — has no mouse-reachable entry point," verify against the running-timer chrome (obs 11 records the sidebar Timer row gaining a live badge + pencil; a focus affordance may live there and was not checked), and that narrower finding can stand at major on strategic grounds rather than frequency. File the P1/None gap and the Ctrl+↵ collision separately as polish.

confirmed.title: The in-product attention budget promotes the funnel and hides the product: every advertised surface sells, every retention feature is invisible
confirmed.evidence: Promoted: obs 6 (fake 'Meeting?' event as calendar-connect ad), obs 44 ('trying 10 Premium features' banner), obs 48 (Invite members illustration dominating an in-use Timeline), design-system.md §8 (mobile-app banner copy), product-map.md §2 & §10 (Upgrade + '31 DAYS' badge, ★ across nav and menus). Hidden: obs 19, 23, 24, 36, 47. Education spent on basics: obs 5, 13, 21; design-system.md §8 (checklist items)
confirmed.argument: Line the two inventories up. Surfaces given pixels, placement, even fabricated calendar events: connect calendar, get the mobile app, invite members, upgrade — acquisition, expansion, conversion. Surfaces given nothing: Focus/Pomodoro (obs 23), Goals (obs 19), the +/#/P1 inline syntax (obs 24 — a power feature with chips that render and strip correctly, and no conceivable organic learning path since the timer bar doesn't even parse it, obs 7), the Unplanned drag-to-plan backlog living in a side rail of the same unlabeled-panel family (obs 47) on a canvas that instead spends its space on an invite promo while in active use (obs 48). So what a user discovers organically is: a timer, plus things to buy. The 'plan seriously' depth that justifies the 2.0 thesis is structurally undiscoverable — a poor trade for a bootstrapped company whose stated scoreboard is retention and expansion, not top-of-funnel (company-research §1, §6).
confirmed.counterargument: This was day one in a near-empty workspace on a 31-day trial: front-loading conversion prompts during a trial is rational, and the SUGGESTED-card engine (obs 5) is precisely the mechanism you would use to stage feature education over the following weeks — a single-day walkthrough cannot observe lifecycle-staged discovery. This is an honest and fairly strong counter; the finding stands on what day one demonstrably teaches, but the imbalance could narrow over time in ways this evidence cannot see.
confirmed.verifierReasoning:
EVIDENCE CHECK — the citations are accurate individually, but the inventory that gives the finding its force does not survive inspection.

The "promoted" list is asserted to be uniformly "acquisition, expansion, conversion." Checked against company-research §4, it is not. **Calendar integrations and focus mode are FREE-tier features** (§4, Free row: "Manual + real-time timers, focus mode, calendar integrations, tasks, boards, task estimates"). So obs 6's calendar-connect card sells nothing — it activates a free feature that feeds the planning canvas, i.e. it is precisely the retention/depth prompt the finding says is absent. The mobile-app banner (design-system §8) is likewise free and is the classic multi-device activation prompt, which for a time tracker is a retention driver, not funnel. "Invite members" (obs 48) is the functional precondition of the surface it appears on: Timeline is a per-person capacity swimlane (product-map §7), and capacity planning across a team of one is degenerate. That leaves the ★ markers and the trial affordances as the only genuine conversion surfaces — and ★ in menus (product-map §10) is honest labeling of what expires, not a sell. Across 57 observations of a live walkthrough the log records **exactly one** hard upgrade CTA (obs 44), non-modal, on a project page, sitting immediately beside obs 43. Half the "every advertised surface sells" inventory is misclassified.

The "hidden" claim is overstated in the other direction. "No conceivable organic learning path" for the inline syntax is refuted by the evaluator's own log: obs 25 proves the `?` shortcut panel documents P1/P2/P3, so the syntax has a documented path via the universal help affordance (obs 22). obs 19 and obs 47 sit behind a toolbar panel toggle; obs 36 sits in a standard ⋮ overflow, which is conventionally where per-object advanced settings live. Every one of the five "hidden" features was found by clicking standard affordances in a single unaided session — which is the opposite of "structurally undiscoverable."

"Every retention feature is invisible" is contradicted by evidence the reviewer read past. obs 43 — the project right rail of value-framed toggles (Recurring / Estimate / Billable / Fixed fee), each a benefit sentence plus a switch, logged as "Strong pattern" — is depth education on prime real estate, immediately adjacent to the obs 44 banner the reviewer counts as pure sell. Add obs 35 (Logged/Planned/Estimate with ⓘ), obs 39 (per-day estimate spread computed onto the board chip), obs 52 (estimate-vs-actual as a first-class report column), obs 46 (the capacity loop closing visibly). The depth layer is surfaced continuously and inline; what it lacks is *proactive* pointing. And obs 5's card reads "Plan tomorrow's first task" — the suggestion engine's day-one output already aims at the plan layer, undercutting "education spent on basics" while simultaneously being the mechanism the reviewer's own counterargument concedes could stage the rest.

SEVERITY — "major" requires real friction in a weekly-or-more path. Discoverability gaps produce non-adoption, not friction; a user who doesn't know Goals exists is not impeded by it. The one weekly surface implicated (the Timer grid, obs 6) carries a single ghost card rendered in the same dashed hypothetical register as the legitimate SUGGESTED card (obs 5) with a "?" in its label and an explicit CTA — visually marked as not-real-data, so "fabricated calendar event" oversells it. obs 48 is a genuine defect but it is a pattern-application bug (design-system §"Empty states": the full-view illustrated pattern persisting after the view has data), not a monetization choice, and real team data would displace it. The tracking hot path itself — obs 11, the running state, logged as "excellent craft" — carries zero promotion.

The reviewer's own counterargument is decisive on the systemic claim and they graded it correctly: one day, one person, empty workspace, day 1 of 31. A single-session snapshot cannot establish an "attention budget" thesis about lifecycle education.

WHAT SURVIVES: a real but much narrower finding. obs 23 is the sharp piece — Focus mode with Pomodoro has no pointer-device entry point anywhere in the chrome, silently no-ops when pressed without a running timer, and depends on shortcuts that need a focus state the user cannot see (obs 27) — and per company-research §4 it is a feature Toggl advertises on its own free tier. Alongside it: the first-run machinery (obs 13, 21) never re-aims past the four checklist basics within the observed session. Those are worth fixing and worth logging as minor. The finding as titled — a funnel capturing the attention budget while retention features are invisible — is not what this evidence shows.

confirmed.title: The project right rail proves the team knows how to make hidden capability discoverable — the pattern just never left the monetized surfaces
confirmed.evidence: obs 43 (Recurring / Estimate / Billable / Fixed fee as benefit-sentence + switch), obs 28 (Repeat appears only after Dates are set), obs 35 (play button on the task title; Time section with Logged/Planned/Estimate)
confirmed.argument: The project Overview right rail is genuinely excellent discoverability design: each capability is a switch paired with one benefit sentence in the user's language ('See how tracked hours compare to your time budget') — the feature explains its own value at the point of use, with zero navigation required (obs 43). Repeat materializing only after Dates exist (obs 28) is progressive disclosure done exactly right, and the play button on a saved task's title (obs 35) surfaces the tracking↔planning bridge at the single most relevant moment. This is the in-house pattern that would solve most findings in this lens.
confirmed.counterargument: The pattern's placement may not be a coincidence: the right rail is precisely the '10 Premium features' surface the trial banner counts (obs 44), so its polish may be conversion-driven rather than evidence of a general discoverability principle. That reading takes nothing away from the craft — but it quietly reinforces the imbalance finding: the best self-explaining UI in the product is where the money is.
confirmed.verifierReasoning:
EVIDENCE CHECK: All three citations are quoted accurately, and the log's own author independently rated each at capture time — obs 43 "Strong pattern," obs 28 "good progressive disclosure," obs 35 "the single best tracking↔planning affordance in the product." The praised behavior is real, and it is textbook-correct practice (value stated at the point of decision, dependent-field disclosure, contextual action on the object), not novelty mistaken for craft. THE PRAISE STANDS AND SHOULD BE KEPT.

What does not survive is the trailing clause — "the pattern just never left the monetized surfaces" — and its restatement in the counterargument ("the best self-explaining UI in the product is where the money is"). Five defenses:

1. THE FINDING'S OWN CITATIONS REFUTE IT. Obs 28 and obs 35 are both the task drawer, a free-tier surface — company-research §4 puts "tasks, boards, task estimates" in Free at $0. Two of the three exhibits offered as proof of a monetization-scoped pattern sit outside the money. Only obs 43 is on a premium-adjacent surface.

2. BENEFIT-FRAMING IS A DOCUMENTED HOUSE VOICE RULE, NOT A RIGHT-RAIL LOCALISM. design-system.md §8 records as a verified read: "Empty states explain the consequence, not just the state: '…to see where your time goes' rather than 'No data'." Free-surface instances exist — "Log time to see where your time goes" on the Summary report (the one non-premium report type, product-map §3) and Members' "Set rates and costs per person — Invite your team to calculate profitability" on an unstarred nav item. The team wrote the principle down as global; obs 43 is its best execution, not its only habitat.

3. THE COUNTERARGUMENT'S PREMISE IS FACTUALLY LOOSE. Obs 44's banner counts "10 Premium features on this project"; the rail carries four toggles. The rail is not "precisely" the surface the banner counts.

4. THE CORRELATION BREAKS ON THE ADJACENT TAB. Obs 45: the project Dashboard — Revenue / Cost / Profit KPIs, the most money-dense surface in the product, one tab over from obs 43 in the same sub-app — carries the worst diagnostic copy in the entire log. "No logged cost — Start by logging time to see progress" when time IS logged and the actual missing input is a member cost rate. If polish tracked revenue, that screen would be the second-best in the product. It is the worst.

5. THE "WOULD SOLVE MOST FINDINGS IN THIS LENS" CLAIM IS A SECOND OVERREACH. Benefit-sentence + switch solves "I see a control and don't know why I'd want it." It does nothing for obs 23 (Focus mode with Pomodoro has no chrome entry point at all) or obs 19 (Goals has no nav placement) — those are missing-control problems, and a benefit sentence attached to nothing is not a fix. It is also irrelevant to obs 14 (always-full Logged bar) and obs 51 (sub-hour rounding to 0h), which are defects, not explanation gaps.

Finally, even granting the strong reading, it is a defense rather than an indictment. Toggl is bootstrapped with zero VC (company-research §1) and its ladder tops out at money questions (§4). Concentrating explanatory craft where conversion and expansion happen is rational resource allocation for that company, not evidence of a principle the team failed to generalize.

RECOMMENDED REFRAME (keep as praise, cut the insinuation): the product has a working in-house pattern for self-explaining controls, best executed in the project right rail (obs 43) and also present on free surfaces (obs 28, 35). The real gap it exposes is narrower and more actionable than "monetization" — the pattern is applied to controls that already exist, and has not been extended into creating entry points for features that have none (obs 23, obs 19). That framing survives the evidence; the monetization framing does not.

minorAndPolish.title: First-run education is three stacked mechanisms, and all three fire simultaneously at the moment of first success
minorAndPolish.argument: A virgin workspace greets the user with three concurrent teaching systems on one surface: a floating checklist, suggested-slot cards, and spotlight tooltips (obs 21). The cards include a fabricated 'MEETING?' ghost event that is actually a calendar-connect ad occupying a working-day slot, and a 'Plan tomorrow's first task' suggestion pinned to Tue 9 AM for no stated reason (obs 5, 6) — so the empty calendar isn't empty; it contains system-authored content before the user has made anything. Then, at the single most important moment of the first session — stopping the first timer — all three systems move at once: spotlight dims the whole UI, a new Logged strip materialises, and the checklist collapses (obs 13). The user's attention at that moment should be on verifying their entry landed; instead the product hijacks it. The checklist also overlaps the sidebar footer at 952px viewport height (obs 12) — the mechanisms even collide spatially, not just temporally.

minorAndPolish.title: The keyboard layer fails silently under exactly first-session conditions, teaching new users that input is unreliable
minorAndPolish.argument: The ? panel proudly documents a deep shortcut layer (obs 22) — then first attempts at using it silently no-op: N does nothing right after navigation until the page has been clicked once (obs 27), F does nothing without a running timer (obs 23), and Ctrl+↵ fails from the Dates field, reopening the date picker instead of saving (obs 26). None of these produce any feedback, so the user cannot distinguish 'broken' from 'not focused' from 'wrong context' — the exact ambiguity that makes people abandon a shortcut layer permanently. This matters more than a generic shortcut papercut because Toggl's first-run population is disproportionately migrated Track and Plan users (company-research §2) — keyboard-habituated people whose first-session judgment is formed by whether muscle memory transfers. Obs 10 hints the lossiness may extend to mouse clicks after popover close (a dead first click on Play, observed twice), which would escalate this to major — but that observation is explicitly not reproduced, so it stands as a flag, not a conviction.

minorAndPolish.title: The empty-state system is disciplined in form but fails in diagnosis: remedy copy that misdiagnoses, an invite prompt that outstays the emptiness, and voice slips against its own rules
minorAndPolish.evidence: obs 45, 48, 57; design-system §7 (two-pattern rule), §8 ('no exclamation marks', empty states 'explain the consequence'); product-map §3 Members; company-research §4
minorAndPolish.argument: The two-pattern empty-state system (inline text vs full-view illustration) is applied consistently — obs 57 confirms a view-level delete lands on the correct illustrated pattern. But the content inside the pattern misfires in ways that hit trial evaluators specifically. The project Dashboard's 'No logged cost — Start by logging time' fires when time IS logged; the actual missing input is a cost rate on the member (obs 45). A user obeying the remedy logs more time, still sees zero, and loses trust in precisely the profitability surface that justifies the Premium price (company-research §4: Starter→Premium is the money-questions gate). Meanwhile Timeline's 'Invite members' illustration still fills the canvas below a lane that is in active use (obs 48) — the full-view pattern deployed against a view that is not empty. And the post-delete empty state ends in an exclamation mark (obs 57), violating the design system's own verified 'no exclamation marks' rule — small, but it means the empty-state layer is drifting from the voice system it belongs to.

minorAndPolish.title: The date picker is a bare month grid with no presets or typed-date affordance, on a field the product's defaults make near-mandatory
minorAndPolish.argument: The picker offers a Mon-first month grid, today outlined, and CLEAR — no today/this-week/+1w presets and no hint that dates can be typed (obs 31). Dates are not optional in practice: the default Tasks view groups by Date (product-map §3, obs 37), the board's columns are date buckets (obs 38), and Repeat only appears after Dates are set (obs 28) — a task without dates is a second-class object, so this picker runs on nearly every task created. Each common case (today, tomorrow, next week) costs grid scanning and clicks. The aggravators: the same drawer's title field already parses natural-language dates (obs 24), so the cheap path exists but is unadvertised inside the picker; and Ctrl+Enter fails from precisely this field (obs 26), stacking the save-shortcut bug on the picker's baseline cost.

minorAndPolish.title: 'Timeline' names two different models — workspace-level people-capacity vs project-level schedule — the one break in an otherwise coherent fractal scoping design
minorAndPolish.argument: A project is a sub-app whose tabs (Tasks/Board/Timeline/Dashboard/Members, obs 41) mirror the global nav almost one-to-one — a deliberate 'project = workspace in miniature' fractal that is mostly a coherence strength. It breaks at Timeline: globally the word means capacity swimlanes per person answering 'who is free' ('40h free', 'No assignee' lane — product-map §3, §7; obs 46, 48), while inside a project it means the schedule answering 'when does work happen' (obs 41). Teams coordinate by view names, so 'check the Timeline' has two referents — and the premium ★ attaches to one of them (product-map §2), so even plan-gating hangs off an ambiguous word.

minorAndPolish.title: 'Board' is a projection of the current group-by — grouped by Date the columns are Overdue/Today/Tue/Wed — not the status kanban its name universally promises; it is also a mode globally but a place inside a project
minorAndPolish.argument: 'Board' carries the industry's strongest prior: status lanes, drag equals status change. Here board columns are the group-by dimension, and the observed default is Date (product-map §3), so first contact with Board shows time columns, not a pipeline (obs 38). The audience most exposed is the migrated Toggl Plan base whose board expectations were set by a different product (company-research §2), and 'boards' is a named free-tier feature (company-research §4), so every plan touches this. Structurally, Board is a view mode of Tasks at workspace level but a destination tab with its own route inside a project (obs 38, 41) — the same word is a toggle at one level and a place at the other.

minorAndPolish.title: Deletion runs on two contracts — confirm-no-undo for the heavier cascading object, undo-no-confirm for the lighter one — while the deleted object's own noun changes mid-product ('time entry' vs 'Time log')
minorAndPolish.evidence: obs 22, 54, 55; design-system §8 ('Start a time entry' checklist string); product-map §3 ('Time logs' report type)
minorAndPolish.argument: Task delete: confirmation modal with consequence copy, no undo afterward (obs 54). Time-entry delete: no confirmation, undo toast (obs 55). A user cannot form one rule — neither 'delete is guarded' nor 'delete is recoverable' holds globally. The risk mapping is inverted: the task cascades ('will remove all related planned time') yet is unrecoverable post-confirm, while the atomic entry gets undo; and since global Ctrl+Z/Ctrl+Y exists (obs 22), it is ambiguous whether task deletion is secretly undoable and merely unadvertised. At the same moment, the noun wobbles: onboarding says 'Start a time entry' (design-system §8), the report menu says 'Time logs' (product-map §3), the toast says 'Time log deleted' (obs 55). The central object of a 15-year time-tracking franchise has no settled name — it reads as a Track→2.0 rename that never finished.

minorAndPolish.title: Residual format and voice leaks — 'Aug 17 - 21' vs 'Aug 17 - Aug 21', '— tap to use' on desktop, one exclamation mark against a no-exclamation register — are cosmetic, not model damage
minorAndPolish.argument: The same date range renders 'Aug 17 - 21' in lists but 'Aug 17 - Aug 21' on board chips and in the drawer (obs 39; format inventory). 'Goals' offers '— tap to use' on a desktop surface (obs 20). The post-delete empty state ends '…get things rolling!' (obs 57) in a product whose measured voice system otherwise verifiably bans exclamation marks and marketing tone entirely (design-system §8: 'No exclamation marks… anywhere in the app chrome'). These are worth logging precisely because Toggl's register is disciplined enough that any leak is conspicuous — but none of them can mislead anyone about how the product works, and this review should say so rather than inflate them.

minorAndPolish.title: The two sides of the seam disagree on the shape of a week and the meaning of shared words
minorAndPolish.argument: The tracking calendar defaults to 5 Days with weekends hidden (obs 3) while the capacity Timeline shows Sat/Sun dimmed (obs 49) — the two surfaces that must reconcile planned against tracked hours render different weeks by default. Vocabulary drifts the same way: the nav says 'Timer' while the URL and tab say 'Calendar' with no on-page title (obs 1, product-map §2); 'Timeline' means capacity lanes globally but project schedule inside a project (obs 41); the Tasks tab title leaks 'Inbox' (obs 40). Each instance is small, but they accumulate into a sense that Track and Plan were built as adjacent products sharing a sidebar rather than one product — which is precisely the perception a 'tracking and planning finally connected' pitch cannot afford.

minorAndPolish.title: Systemic vocabulary drift: one product speaks at least five conflicting dialects, in violation of its own codified voice system
minorAndPolish.evidence: obs 1, 20, 25, 40, 55, 57; Format inventory section ("Aug 17 - 21" vs "Aug 17 - Aug 21"); design-system.md §8 ("no exclamation marks"); product-map.md §1; company-research.md §2 (Plan→Focus→2.0 migration)
minorAndPolish.argument: The tracking surface has three identities — nav "Timer", URL/tab "Calendar", no on-page title (obs 1). The Tasks tab title leaks "Inbox" (obs 40). The shortcuts panel says priorities are "P1 P2 P3" while the priority menu says High/Medium/Low/None — two user-facing surfaces, disjoint vocabularies for one feature (obs 25). The delete toast introduces "Time log" as a third term for time entry (obs 55). "— tap to use" ships on desktop (obs 20), and the post-delete empty state uses an exclamation mark (obs 57) in a product whose observed voice system explicitly has none (design-system §8: "No exclamation marks... anywhere in the app chrome"). Individually papercuts; together they show the copy system — which is genuinely codified and disciplined on primary surfaces — has no enforcement on triggered and edge surfaces, exactly the surfaces the design-system doc flagged UNVERIFIED at extraction. For a company grading candidates on copy detail, the drift is the tell that the discipline is per-surface, not systemic.

minorAndPolish.title: The board's most distinctive capability presents itself as a bug: columns are the group-by dimension, and nothing on the board says so
minorAndPolish.evidence: obs 38, 39; product-map.md §3 (Board is a mode of Tasks; 'Board view columns and behaviour' was an open item); company-research.md §2 (Plan users were force-migrated ~Oct 2025, expectations set by a different tool)
minorAndPolish.argument: Grouped by Date, the board's lanes are Overdue / Today / Tue / Wed (obs 38) — not the status lanes that 'board' universally implies. The generative model (lanes = whatever Group by says) is genuinely more powerful than fixed kanban, and the cards are excellent (computed per-day estimate spread, obs 39) — but nothing on the board surface labels the lanes as group-by output; the explanation lives in a toolbar control visually detached from the columns. The audience most likely to hit this is the migrated Plan base, users who did not choose this product and arrive expecting kanban; for them a date-grouped board reads as a broken status board, and the differentiator is experienced as a defect.

result.critic:
## 1. Evidence not represented by any finding

**Uncited observations: 2, 9, 34, 42, 53, 56.**
- **obs 34** — the `Task created` toast has no action link, while the *delete* toast carries UNDO (obs 55). Creation is the one flow with no route back to its object — sharpens the destructive-asymmetry finding.
- **obs 42** — alerts, milestones, "Complete project", Draft: four project-lifecycle features seen and never opened.
- **obs 53** — the whole notification system. No finding asks whether the product ever proactively tells a user anything (timer still running, estimate exceeded).
- **obs 2** — idle timer renders `0:00:00`: a tenth duration format, counted in the inventory but never named as a defect.
- **obs 9, 56** — client-grouped project picker, skeletons-not-spinners. Uncredited craft.

**Corpus-level:** no accessibility pass at all (contrast, focus visibility, tab order, reduced motion, SR) despite the keyboard layer being a *major*. The AI surface (Tasks ✨, ✨ IMPORT TASKS, three shipped AI animations — design-system §6) is untouched. Two verified code defects are unclaimed: GT Haptik fetched and never applied plus a dead bundler alias (§3), and `--*-data-light/dark` never defined (§2). Admin settings unopened — **Targets may be the same object as Goals**, which would change that finding.

## 2. Caveats a reviewer must know

- **Single user, single day, 28s of data, one project/task.** Every "reads as zero" finding is a low-data-regime claim; obs 51 concedes ≥1h is fine. Variance, Time status, estimate-vs-actual, forecasts, Workload/Utilization/Profitability never rendered populated.
- **Premium trial** — the Free boundary (where "focus mode" is sold) was never observed. **Time off paywalled even on trial; Approvals never exercised.**
- **No second member** — assignee≠self, "No assignee" lane, roles/permissions, and the obs 45 remedy (setting a member rate) are all untested.
- **Dark theme only; desktop only; one viewport** (952px height). No mobile despite "tap to use" and the mobile-app banner.
- **Untested mechanisms:** global Ctrl+Z (the entire undo-based delete contract), CSV import, saved views, filters, search, sidebar collapse, org/workspace switch, error/offline/validation states, timers across midnight, timezone/DST, idle detection.
- obs 10 (dead click) is explicitly unreproduced.

## 3. Findings that are the same issue

Merge: the four **0h/rounding** items (13,14,16,50,51). Five **hidden-feature-tier** items → one root: no visible entry, silent failure (19,22,23,27) — the two **Goals** items collapse into it. Two **drawer draft-loss** items (32). Two **auto-log** items (36). Two **Board group-by** items (38). Four **running-timer praise** items (11,35). Keyboard-fails-silently appears three times; vocabulary drift, twice. ~34 findings compress to roughly 15.
